extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators, middle-level teachers, and program designers
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and operating a graduate-level professional development/master's program for middle-level mathematics teachers that integrates mathematical content, pedagogy, action research, and capstone requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular homework practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Homework is assigned, collected, reviewed, and graded (in some fashion) regularly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematics homework assignments include a variety of problems, ranging from computational to those requiring extensive problem solving, explanation, and mathematical justification. Participants are encouraged to collaborate on assignments in whatever groups they choose but to submit their work individually.

rubrics_metrics.name: End-of-course assignment requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical End-of-Course Assignment includes careful explanations for solutions to a set of problems selected by the teacher; reflections about the nature of course learning; and solutions to an 'End of Course Problem Set.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers may submit solutions, receive feedback, and revise; assignments emphasize helping teachers reach a point where they can successfully solve the problems assigned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-group instructional structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Most courses divide participants into roughly five subgroups, each assigned to a member of the instructional team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groups convene daily (during on-site courses) to provide an intimate atmosphere for discussing daily homework, course content questions, and other concerns; small groups support participants who are hesitant to present before an entire class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of technology in courses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of technology is part of many courses, online or face-to-face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All participants receive a TI-84 Plus Silver Edition calculator (used to graph complex functions); courses use MapleTA (online assessment), Microsoft Excel, and GeoGebra (dynamic geometry linked with algebra and calculus). Technology is used as a tool for exploring more complicated mathematics and for assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action research project (Master's Exam component)
rubrics_metrics.description: An action research project and report is a Master's program requirement for MA students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers identify a problem of practice, read research articles, develop an inquiry plan, collect data as they implement the plan, and reflect on practices and the plan while analyzing results. Participants plan projects in TEAC 888 and submit IRB proposals before conducting research; a report on the action research is a degree requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expository mathematics paper (MAT requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: MAT students write an expository paper on a mathematics topic assigned by the faculty as part of the Master's requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each MAT student receives a different topic, uses available resources (internet, library, and mathematicians) to learn about the topic, and writes an expository paper accessible to peers; these expository papers represent efforts to learn new mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capstone oral exam requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The capstone course concludes with two days of oral exams during which participants give a talk about their action research paper (MA) or their mathematics expository paper (MAT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oral exams are part of the Master's Exam requirements and are used to assess integration of mathematics and pedagogy learned in the program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical habits of mind — understands which tools are appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Understands which tools are appropriate when solving a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the project's working definition of Mathematical Habits of Mind; these dispositions are intended to be operationalized and identified in multiple contexts (teachers as learners, students as learners) and inform course goals and tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical habits of mind — thinks flexibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Thinks flexibly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included in the working definition of a mathematical thinker; informs expectation that tasks allow multiple approaches and adaptability of thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical habits of mind — uses precise definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses precise mathematical definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages emphasis on precision in definitions and language as part of coursework and student work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical habits of mind — recognizes multiple solution paths
rubrics_metrics.description: Understands that there exist multiple paths to a solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informs selection of 'Habits of Mind problems' and classroom tasks that are solvable in several ways to promote flexible reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical habits of mind — makes connections to prior knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Is able to make connections between prior knowledge and the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courses build from basic to more sophisticated material and emphasize connecting new ideas to prior knowledge (e.g., arithmetic to algebra to geometry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical habits of mind — identifies crucial information
rubrics_metrics.description: Knows what information in the problem is crucial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction and problems should require discerning relevant vs. irrelevant information as part of mathematical problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical habits of mind — develops strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Is able to develop strategies to solve a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem sets and Habits of Mind problems should promote strategy development, experimentation, and recursive thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical habits of mind — explains solutions to others
rubrics_metrics.description: Is able to explain solutions to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courses emphasize communication of mathematical ideas (writing, presentations, group discussion) and include assignments that require explanation and justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical habits of mind — knows algorithm effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Knows the effectiveness of algorithms within the context of the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotes understanding when algorithms are appropriate, their limitations, and context-dependent effectiveness rather than rote application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical habits of mind — persistence in problem solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Is persistent in finding a solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course design and problems should foster persistence and sustained engagement with challenging tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical habits of mind — displays self-efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Displays self-efficacy while doing problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs should build confidence through scaffolded challenges, feedback, and opportunities for revision and success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical habits of mind — engages in metacognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Engages in meta-cognition by monitoring and reflecting on the processes of conjecturing, reasoning, proving, and problem solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflections, research reports, and course assignments are intended to develop metacognitive awareness and reflection on mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of 'Habits of Mind' problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems that foster mathematical habits of mind are accessible without demanding a strong mathematics background, need not be connected to the current mathematics being studied, and ideally can be solved in several ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good problems allow experimentation with data or special cases, require careful reasoning and creativity before a thorough solution, are 'fun', and can be adapted for classroom use; these problems emphasize problem solving, careful reasoning, and effective communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum sequencing principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Program starts with a basic course and becomes increasingly more sophisticated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designed with the expectation many participants have elementary-teacher backgrounds or long gaps since taking math courses; sequencing builds foundational understanding before advanced topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairing math content with pedagogy courses
rubrics_metrics.description: Courses are often taken in pairs: a course in mathematics followed by one that explores its teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pairing supports transfer of mathematical learning into planned and enacted curriculum and aligns with TLTE/MA program goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for diverse participant backgrounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Courses are designed to offer challenging and coherent mathematics while being accessible to participants with varied backgrounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of Habits of Mind problems, technology, small groups, and opportunities for revision help make rigorous content accessible to all participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment limitations and evaluation caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Measuring program impact on student achievement is complicated by varied district tests, ceiling effects on CRTs, and weak overlap between standardized test content and the program's focus on habits of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value-added models require baseline student scores; small sample linkage to student scores and CRT ceiling effects can prevent estimation of teacher effects. These limitations should be considered when evaluating program efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course design connecting advanced topics to middle-level curricula
rubrics_metrics.description: Advanced topics (e.g., number theory, cryptology) are developed with connections to middle-level curricula and proofs are chosen to be relevant and accessible to middle-level teachers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include elementary ciphers or applications (e.g., RSA) to show real-world relevance and create enrichment activities adaptable for middle-level students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling best teaching practices in program delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Program instructors model best practices: activities and group work, appropriate technology, student research on history, and student projects/presentations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courses aim to model pedagogies teachers can use in their classrooms, including the use of CBMS- and NCTM-aligned materials and interactive tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory definition of 'Highly Qualified Teacher' for Maryland
rubrics_metrics.description: To be considered a highly qualified middle school math teacher (new hires after Jan 8, 2002), one must hold a bachelor's degree, a valid teaching certificate, and either pass the Praxis II middle school math test or have completed a major (or equivalent) in mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experienced teachers hired before Jan 8, 2002 must meet these requirements or earn enough points under Maryland's 'High, Objective, Uniform State Standard of Evaluation' rubric; program design should help teachers meet these state requirements.
